750.title: Tamar (2 Samuel 13)
750.hook: a king's daughter is violated and silenced; the text names the wrong plainly
750.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Tamar as part of the book of Samuel; some teachers today use it to talk openly about sexual violence and about believing those who come forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday David rose from the ground after his child died. Your line was I shall go to him. A new week begins, and today's story is a hard one.

A note before we begin: today's story is about sexual violence. It's told without detail, and if you need to stop, that's fine. Tamar is a daughter of King David, the sister of Absalom. Her half-brother Amnon becomes fixated on her. His cousin and friend Jonadab hands him a plan: pretend to be sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for you. David sends her. She kneads the dough in front of her brother and bakes the cakes. She has no reason to be afraid.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER.` → `A PLAN TO GET HER ALONE.` → `SHE COMES TO COOK.`

segments.voice: Amnon sends everyone out and takes hold of her. The first thing to notice: Tamar speaks. She says no. This is not done in Israel, she says; do not do this wanton thing. She asks where she could carry her shame, and what he would become. She even offers a way out: speak to the king; he will not keep me from you. He will not listen. He is stronger, and he forces her. Then, the text says, he hates her more than he had loved her, and has her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar doesn't go quietly. She tears the long robe the king's unmarried daughters wore, puts ashes on her head, lays her hand on it, and goes away crying aloud. The second thing to notice: the Bible names this as a wrong. It doesn't blur it or blame her. It gives her words, and records her grief in public. Then the silencing. Absalom says: hold your peace, my sister; he is your brother; don't take this to heart. And Tamar "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house. King David hears all of it and is very angry. The text doesn't say he does anything. Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, and waits. Much of what follows grows out of that silence: a murder, a rebellion, a war between father and son. Why is this chapter here? In a palace where the powerful wanted it quiet, the text remembers her name, her words, and her torn robe. Her story is told.

segments.voice: Think of someone who might one day bring you something painful, and picture yourself listening without what Absalom said: not hush, not don't take it to heart, just I believe you, and I'm here. If this story touched your own life, simply breathe, and know that yours deserves to be told too. If you pray, you can remember Tamar and everyone like her.
Tamar. A king's daughter who said no, was wronged, and was told to be quiet, and whose story the text refused to drop. Today's word.
Your line: her story is told. The text refused to let it be hushed. Until tomorrow, gently.

751.title: He stole their hearts (2 Samuel 15:1–6)
751.hook: Absalom wins the people at the gate with flattery
751.carry: a kiss, a nod, a sigh
751.howItsDone: Jews read Absalom at the gate as part of the book of Samuel, and later Jewish teaching uses a related phrase, genevat da'at, stealing the mind, for misleading someone.

segments.voice: Yesterday Tamar said no, and was told to hold her peace. Your line was her story is told. Today, her brother Absalom stands at the city gate, smiling.

Early morning at the gate of Jerusalem. A farmer has walked in from his town with a dispute, a boundary line, a debt, a stolen animal, to bring it to the king. Before he reaches anyone official, a handsome young man steps out from beside the road. Where are you from? The farmer tells him. The young man hears his case and nods. Your matters are good and right, he says. Then he lowers his voice. But there's no one from the king to hear you.
screen: `DAWN AT THE GATE.` → `A MAN WITH A CASE.` → `YOUR MATTERS ARE GOOD AND RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The young man is Absalom. Since Tamar, a lot has happened. He waited, had Amnon killed, and fled. Years later he was allowed home, and his father kissed him. Now he gets a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him, and goes to work at the gate. Look at his method. He rises early and stands beside the road. He asks each person where they're from. He tells every one of them their case is good and right, with only one side in front of him, and says the king has no one to listen. Then he sighs aloud: oh, that I were made judge in the land! Anyone with a cause could come to me, and I'd give them justice. When someone bows to him, he won't allow it; he takes hold of them and kisses them. Every move is warm. Every move is aimed. The text sums it up: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." The same Hebrew phrase, to steal a heart, appears in Genesis when Jacob slips away from Laban without telling him, and there it means fooling him. So the line has two edges: Absalom won their affection, and he did it by fooling them. He doesn't lie about everything. Maybe the courts really were slow. Maybe people really did feel unheard. He takes a real grievance and makes himself the answer, and he never has to decide a single case. Saying yes to everyone is easy when you never have to rule.

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days to a moment when someone told you exactly what you wanted to hear, an ad, a voice online, a friend who agreed a little too fast, and ask the farmer's question: did they hear the other side? Then turn it around, gently, to a moment when you said only what someone wanted to hear; no need to judge it, just see it clearly.

752.title: Up the hill, weeping (2 Samuel 15:30)
752.hook: the fleeing king climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered
752.carry: he let the hard day be hard
752.howItsDone: Jews read David's flight from Jerusalem as part of the book of Samuel; the heading of Psalm 3 links that psalm to the time David fled from Absalom his son.

segments.voice: Yesterday Absalom stole the lev, the heart, of everyone at the gate. Your line was a kiss, a nod, a sigh. Today, those stolen hearts become a revolt, and his father leaves the city on foot.

A messenger runs into the palace with one sentence: the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom. Absalom has had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, and he's coming. David doesn't try to hold the city. Arise, he says, let us flee, or none of us will escape him. So the king of Israel walks out of his own city, his household behind him, crosses the brook Kidron, and starts up the slope on the far side. Not riding. Walking. Barefoot.
screen: `THE HEARTS ARE AFTER ABSALOM.` → `ARISE, LET US FLEE.` → `ACROSS THE KIDRON, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: The verse is a slow picture. David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and "wept as he went up". His head was covered. He went barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads too, and went up weeping. Some readers see a mourner in the covered head and bare feet. The king who once danced before the ark with all his might now climbs a hill like a mourner. In Hebrew the verse keeps saying the same two things: going up, weeping, one step at a time. What's striking is what David does on the way. He doesn't give up. He sends the priests back to the city with the ark: if I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, God will bring me back and let me see it again. And if not, here I am; let God do to me what seems good. Then he hears that Ahithophel, his own wise counselor, has joined Absalom, and he prays a short, practical prayer: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. At the top, where God was worshipped, a loyal friend named Hushai is waiting, his coat torn and earth on his head, and David gives him a job. So the climb is two things at once. It is grief, honest and out loud, in front of everyone. And it is still movement. Weeping didn't stop David walking, and walking didn't stop him weeping.

753.title: Let him curse (2 Samuel 16:5–13)
753.hook: Shimei curses the fleeing king; David will not strike back
753.carry: one choice, on one road, to keep walking
753.howItsDone: Jews read Shimei's cursing as part of the book of Samuel; the Talmud praises those who are insulted and do not insult back, and David on the road to Bahurim is one picture of that restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday David climbed the Mount of Olives, barefoot, his head covered. Your line was he let the hard day be hard. Today, beyond that hill, someone is waiting with stones.
screen: `HE LET THE HARD DAY BE HARD.`

segments.voice: Stones. That's the first thing David's people notice at Bahurim: stones flying at them from the hillside. Then the voice. A man named Shimei, son of Gera, from the family of Saul, walks along the ridge above the road, throwing rocks and dust and shouting. Get out, get out, you man of blood! The Lord has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, whose throne you took. Now the kingdom is your son's. Below him walks the king, his mighty men on his right hand and on his left.
screen: `STONES FROM THE HILLSIDE.` → `SHIMEI OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL.` → `YOU MAN OF BLOOD!`

segments.voice: Abishai, one of David's commanders, has heard enough. Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head. David says no, and his answer comes in layers. First: what have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Then: "let him curse", because maybe the Lord has told him to curse David, and who could then ask, why have you done so? Then the line that shows where David's mind is: my own son seeks my life; how much more this man from Benjamin? Leave him alone. And finally a hope: maybe the Lord will look on my affliction, and repay me good for this cursing today. So they keep walking, and Shimei keeps pace along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, flinging dust. David doesn't say Shimei is right, and neither does the narrator. But David once heard thou art the man, and some readers hear that in his answer: a king who knows he isn't innocent, letting an insult go by without needing to win it. There's an honest wrinkle. Much later, on his deathbed, David tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless. The text keeps that too. The restraint on the road was real; it wasn't the whole of David. That makes the moment more useful, not less. Letting one insult go doesn't require being a saint.

754.title: O Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 19:1)
754.hook: the king weeps for the son who rebelled: "would I had died for thee"
754.carry: would I had died for thee
754.tomorrow: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
754.howItsDone: Jews read David's lament for Absalom as part of the book of Samuel; in Jewish Bibles the cry is the opening verse of chapter 19, while English Bibles that follow the King James numbering place it at the end of chapter 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday Shimei threw stones from the ridge, and David kept walking. Your line was one choice, on one road, to keep walking. Today, the war with Absalom ends, and the news reaches his father.
screen: `ONE CHOICE, ON ONE ROAD, TO KEEP WALKING.`

segments.voice: Before the battle, the king stands at the gate as his army marches out, and gives one order, loud enough for every soldier to hear: deal gently, for my sake, with the young man, with Absalom. The fighting is in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest, the text says, devours more people than the sword. A watchman on the wall sees a runner. Then another. David has one question for each of them, and it isn't about the battle. Is the young man Absalom safe?
screen: `DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.` → `THE FOREST OF EPHRAIM.` → `IS ABSALOM SAFE?`

segments.voice: He wasn't. Riding a mule under a great oak, Absalom caught his head fast in the tree, and the mule went on, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth. A soldier saw him and wouldn't touch him, because of the king's order. Joab didn't hesitate. Absalom died there, and they threw him into a pit in the forest and heaped stones over him. The second runner, a Cushite, answers the king in the gentlest words he can find: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. David understands. He is shaken, and goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he goes he says: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! "would I had died for thee", O Absalom, my son, my son! Over Saul and Jonathan, David made a song. Here there is no song, only broken words circling back to one: my son. This is the son who stole the people's hearts, drove his father barefoot out of the city, and came after his life. David's grief has no conditions. He doesn't say, if only he hadn't rebelled. He wishes he had died in his place. It doesn't stay private. The victory turns to mourning, and soldiers slip back into the city like people ashamed after a defeat. Joab tells the king bluntly he is shaming the men who saved his life. And David gets up and sits in the gate. A father's grief that holds nothing back, and a king who still has to face his people.

755.title: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
755.hook: a woman on the wall saves her town with a few wise words
755.carry: one wise voice saves a city
755.howItsDone: Jews read the wise woman of Abel as part of the book of Samuel; some readers set her beside the wise woman of Tekoa in chapter 14, and one midrash identifies her with Serah, the daughter of Asher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry from the room over the gate: my son, my son. Your line was would I had died for thee. Today the kingdom is still cracking, and one voice from a town wall saves a town.

The battering has already started. Absalom is dead, but the kingdom hasn't settled. A man named Sheba son of Bichri has blown a trumpet and shouted: we have no part in David. Joab, back at the head of David's army, has chased him to a walled town called Abel of Beth-maacah. Sheba is inside. The army has thrown up a siege mound against the town, and the soldiers are battering the wall. Everyone inside is about to pay for one man. Then, from the top of the wall, a woman calls out.
screen: `WE HAVE NO PART IN DAVID.` → `A SIEGE AT ABEL.` → `A VOICE FROM THE WALL.`

segments.voice: The text calls her a wise woman, and never gives her name. Her first words: hear, hear! Tell Joab to come near, so I can speak with him. And Joab comes. She doesn't scream at the army or hide in a cellar. She asks for a conversation with the one person who can stop it. Are you Joab? I am. Then listen to the words of your handmaid. I'm listening. And she makes her case. First, the town's name: in the old days people said, ask counsel at Abel, and so they settled things. Second, who she is: one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel. Third, what Joab is about to do: you seek to destroy a city and "a mother in Israel". Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the Lord? Joab answers fast. Far be it from me! One man, Sheba, has lifted his hand against the king. Hand him over, and I'll leave. She says: his head will be thrown to you over the wall. Then she goes to all the people, the text says, in her wisdom. They do it. Joab blows the trumpet, and the army goes home. It's a grim ending, and the text doesn't soften it. But a whole town was about to fall for one man's rebellion. She found out what the commander actually wanted, named what was at stake, and found the narrow way through. The text records no other voice from that wall. Hers was enough.

Ask the wise woman's questions: who can actually stop this, what do they really want, what's at stake that they might not see? Then shape one calm, clear sentence and just have it ready; if you pray, you can ask for wise words.
Wise woman. The unnamed woman on Abel's wall who asked for the commander and spoke for her city. Today's word.

756.title: David's last words (2 Samuel 23:1–4)
756.hook: one who rules justly is "as the light of the morning"
756.howItsDone: Jews read David's last words as part of the book of Samuel; David is remembered in Jewish tradition as the sweet singer of Israel, and some psalms carry his name in their headings.

segments.voice: Yesterday the wise woman on Abel's wall called for the commander and saved her town. Your line was one wise voice saves a city. Today, near the end of Samuel, David's own voice, in a poem.

After the rooftop, the ewe lamb, the child, Tamar, the climb, the cry over the gate, the book gives David a short poem and calls it his last words. It opens like a signature. David the son of Jesse says. The man raised up on high says. The anointed of the God of Jacob. The sweet singer of Israel. Then he says where the words come from: the spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue. What he passes on is a picture of what a ruler should be.
screen: `AFTER EVERYTHING, A POEM.` → `THE SON OF JESSE SAYS.` → `HIS WORD WAS ON MY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: one who rules over people must be just, ruling in the fear of God. Then the image. He shall be "as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth", a morning without clouds, like tender grass springing out of the earth by clear shining after rain. Justice in this poem isn't a sword or a gavel. It's daylight. Morning light doesn't choose whose field to shine on. A fair ruler, read this way, lets everyone underneath grow. Now hold that next to the man saying it: the king who took another man's wife, arranged a death, heard what was done to his daughter Tamar and, as far as the text says, did nothing, and whose own son rose against him. The poem erases none of that. Beside his story, it reads as an ideal his own life shows is hard to reach. The next line can be heard two ways. Some translations have David admit that his house is not so with God; the Jewish translation of 1917 hears a question: is not my house so with God? Either way, the line ends on an everlasting covenant God has made with him. One honest note: the opening of the book of Kings records later instructions from David to Solomon. Perhaps these are his last words as a poet, or the book's chosen farewell. Either way, the words it labels last are not about battles. They are about light.
screen: `RULING JUSTLY, IN THE FEAR OF GOD.` · then, large: `AS THE LIGHT OF THE MORNING.` · then: `GRASS AFTER RAIN.` · `AN IDEAL HE REACHED FOR.`

segments.voice: You're in charge of something, even if it's small: a household, a team, a classroom, a dog. Picture the people in it and ask whether someone gets less of your light: less patience, less benefit of the doubt. If you pray, you can hold David's picture: the light of the morning.
